newsitem.title: FRANCE: French moves may push BAe towards GEC - paper.
newsitem.headline: French moves may push BAe towards GEC - paper.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc (BAe) could move closer to Britain's General Electric Co Plc (GEC) and Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa) if France took a nationalist approach in its defence industry restructuring, chief executive Sir Richard Evans said on Thursday.

Evans said he favoured horizontal alliances across Europe, bringing together airframe makers on one side and makers of missiles and electronics on the other, although U.S. companies had shown it was possible to combine the two sides.

"But if France took a strictly national approach, we would not exclude moving closer to British electronics group GEC. We could also envisage moving closer to Dasa, along the lines mentioned above, which the French could join later; but that would not be the best solution," he said in an interview with French daily Le Monde.
BAe continued to support a bid by French conglomerate Lagardere for the state's majority stake in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, through its Matra-BAe Dynamics missiles joint venture, he said.

BAe and Lagardere had bid for Dasa's missiles business which was for sale, he said. If BAe-Matra had both the missiles interests of Thomson-CSF and Dasa, it could face the U.S. competition head-on, he said.
France's state-owned Aerospatiale could also sell its missile activities to the group if it wanted, he added.

Evans reiterated his view of a future single pan-European contractor which would imply the disappearance of Aerospatiale, BAe and Dasa. But contrary to the fears of the French, the question of control of capital would not be a problem as shareholders in each of the three companies would exchange their shares for shares in the new company.
Analysts have long speculated over a merger between BAe and GEC, which would create a British behemoth with a combined market value of 15.6 billion sterling ($25.4 billion).

Evans urged the French government to lose no time in the industry restructuring, as a year had been lost on the Thomson-CSF privatisation and nine months had shown "nothing concrete" in the Dassault-Aerospatiale merger negotiations. It had only taken two weeks for Boeing and McDonnell Douglas to decide to merge, he said.
"European industry cannot afford to wait much longer," he said.
